messages.text: **Starting a new project.** I'll ask a few questions to set it up: your source database, where the code comes from, and how to convert it. They're on the card below, one at a time. Submit when you've answered them all.

options.description: Azure Synapse, BigQuery, Snowflake (data validation only), or a code conversion only source: IBM Db2, Sybase IQ, Spark SQL, Databricks SQL, Greenplum, Netezza, Vertica or Hive. Type the name.

1... ---
2... name: add-code-units
3... description: Add local source code files to a migration project using scai code add. Use when source SQL files are already available on disk instead of extracting from a live database. Triggers: add code, import files, local files, add source, scai code add.
4... parent_skill: register-code-units
5... license: Proprietary. See License-Skills for complete terms
6... ---
7... 
8... # Add Local Source Code
9... 
10... ## On Entry
11... 
12... Tell the user:
13... > **Importing local SQL files.**
14... >
15... > I'll handle this for you — importing your local SQL files and organizing them by type into `source/`, ready for conversion. It's a single automated step; you won't need to copy, arrange, or move anything yourself.
16... 
17... ## Prerequisites
18... 
19... - Migration project initialized (`scai init`)
20... - Local directory containing SQL source files
21... 
22... ## Workflow
23... 
24... ### Step 1: Get Source Path
25... 
26... If the session's `workload` is `dbt`, load `dbt.md` instead of Steps 1–4, then rejoin at Step 5.
27... 
28... Otherwise, ask the user for the path to their source SQL files:
29... 
30... > "Where are your SQL source files located? Please provide the full path to the directory."
31... 
32... ### Step 2: Annotate Multi-Object Files with sc-tags
33... 
34... `scai code add` uses the arrange engine to split files into one object per code unit. For non-T-SQL dialects the engine splits on `/* <sc-...> */` boundary tags. Before importing, call the `split_code` MCP tool to detect files that need tags (at least one top-level object and no SC tag yet) and inject those tags automatically. Files that already carry SC tags, such as Teradata extraction-script output, are copied unchanged.
35... 
36... ```
37... split_code(input_path="<INPUT_PATH>")
38... ```
39... 
40... - If no file needs tags, the tool says so and you can skip ahead to Step 3 using `<INPUT_PATH>` directly.
41... - Otherwise the tool copies all files to `artifacts/source_split/` (leaving out macOS `__MACOSX/` / `._*` metadata), injects the sc-tags, verifies the result, and tells you to use `artifacts/source_split` as the input for Step 3.
42... - If it lists files that still have no SC tag, apply the fix it gives for each before Step 3 — do not fall back to `--code-already-split`.
43... 
44... The tool handles the full detect → inject → verify cycle in one call. It is OS-agnostic and does not require Python.
45... 
46... **Example** — what the tool injects before each object in a multi-object file:
47... 
48... ```sql
49... /* <sc-table>sales.public.customers</sc-table> */
50... CREATE TABLE sales.public.customers (
51...   id INT,
52...   name VARCHAR(100)
53... );
54... 
55... /* <sc-view>sales.public.v_active_customers</sc-view> */
56... CREATE VIEW sales.public.v_active_customers AS
57... SELECT * FROM sales.public.customers WHERE active = 1;
58... ```
59... 
60... > **T-SQL note:** T-SQL files do not need this step — the engine has a native T-SQL splitter. Skip Step 2 for T-SQL source files.
61... 
62... ### Step 2b: Give SQL Server files their database
63... 
64... **SQL Server only; skip for every other dialect and for dbt.** An object belongs to the database
65... named by the `USE` in effect where it is defined. A file with no `USE` puts its objects in
66... `defaultdb`, where same-named objects from different databases collide and cross-database
67... references (`SALES.dbo.ORDERS`) find no unit. Give `code add` each file's database instead:
68... `--database <NAME>` for the whole input, or `--database-map <FILE>` per path. It writes the
69... `USE` into the engine's copy only (the user's files and `artifacts/source_raw/` stay as they were)
70... and records the assignment under `.scai/code-add/`.
71... 
72... 1. Count the files that already name their database:
73...    `grep -rliE '^[[:space:]]*USE[[:space:]]' <INPUT_PATH> | wc -l` against the `.sql` count (UTF-16
74...    files do not match `grep`; check those by opening them). If every file has one, skip to Step 3. A file's own `USE` always wins over an assignment.
75... 2. Collect the evidence for the rest, never guessing a name:
76...    - **Layout:** top-level folders or file-name prefixes per database (`<DB>/…`, `<DB>_db__…`), or a
77...      `.sqlproj` (the engine binds those itself; leave them unassigned).
78...    - **References:** the first part of three-part names in the code
79...      (`grep -rhoiE '\[?[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*\]?\.\[?[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*\]?\.\[?[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*' <INPUT_PATH> | cut -d. -f1 | sort | uniq -c`),
80...      SSIS connection `Initial Catalog` values, deploy scripts, and the source connection's databases
81...      when one is configured.
82... 3. Classify the input and act:
83...    - **S1, layout names the databases:** each folder or prefix matches a database the references or
84...      the source name. Write the map (one rule per folder or prefix, first match wins) to
85...      `.scai/config/database-map.json` (not under `artifacts/`, which a failed add only cleans when it
86...      was empty), e.g. `{"databases": [{"path": "**/SALES_ARCHIVE_db__*", "database":
87...      "SALES_ARCHIVE"}, {"path": "SALES", "database": "SALES"}]}`. Put the narrower
88...      rules first. Show the user the folder → database table and ask with `ask_user_question` to
89...      confirm or correct it.
90...    - **One database, flat dump:** ask for the database's name and pass `--database <NAME>`. The
91...      answer is a name: when the evidence suggests names (a three-part-name prefix, the source
92...      connection's databases), offer them as `ask_user_question` options; when it suggests none,
93...      ask in a plain message and wait for the typed name, as Step 1 asks for the path. Leaving the
94...      files without a database is never the only option offered: it puts them in `defaultdb`.
95...    - **S2, several databases, no layout:** propose what the references support, file by file, and
96...      ask. Never assign a database the evidence does not name.
97...    - **S6, a deployment merged or renamed databases** (folders say `STAGE` but file prefixes say
98...      `STAGE` and `STAGE_JL`): ask which model is migrated, the original databases (prefix
99...      rules) or the deployed ones (folder rules). Code that references the deployed names binds
100...      only under the deployed model; copies that collide inside a merged database are then S4.
101...    - **S5, environment copies** (`SALES_DEV`, `SALES_QA`, `SALES_PROD`): ask whether to migrate one
102...      environment (map only its folder and leave the others out of the input) or all of them as
103...      separate databases.
104... 4. Check the plan without changing anything:
105...    `scai code add -i <INPUT_PATH> --database-map .scai/config/database-map.json --dry-run --json`.
106...    `result.databaseAssignments` lists each file's `database` and `source` (`map`, `option`, or
107...    `file` for its own `USE`; `assignedDatabase` then names the assignment it overrode). `ADD0026`
108...    means a rule matched no file, `ADD0033` that an earlier rule takes every file it matches: fix
109...    the pattern or move the narrower rule first, never drop the rule silently. Then run Step 3 with
110...    the same option.
111... 
112... ### Step 3: Add Code to Project
113... 
114... Use the path returned by `split_code` (or `<INPUT_PATH>` directly if no file needed tags).
115... 
116... Launch this call as the next section says: `run_in_background=true`, or set the bash tool `timeout` to at least `900000` (15 minutes), then poll until the command finishes. The default 120 second timeout kills the process during the conversion engine's silent pause and a relaunch starts it over.
117... 
118... ```bash
119... scai code add -i <INPUT_PATH> --json
120... ```
121... 
122... With Step 2b's assignment, add the same `--database <NAME>` or `--database-map <FILE>`.
123... 
124... **dbt projects use this form instead** — always, with no exceptions:
125... 
126... ```bash
127... scai code add -i <DBT_PROJECT_PATH> --code-already-split --json
128... ```
129... 
130... Step 2 is skipped for dbt, so the files have no SC tags; `--code-already-split` tells the arrange
131... engine the input is already one object per file. Without it the command fails with `ADD0010`.
132... 
133... This will:
134... - Copy all files from the input path to `artifacts/source_raw/`
135... - Arrange and process the source code
136... - Merge processed output into `source/`
137... 
138... **If files already exist** and you need to overwrite:
139... ```bash
140... scai code add -i <INPUT_PATH> --overwrite --json
141... ```
142... 
143... #### If the import times out or runs in the background
144... 
145... This section covers every `scai code add` the register and conversion skills run: the SQL
146... add here, ETL, dbt, Power BI and `code-conversion-only`.
147... 
148... Launch the command with `run_in_background=true`, or set the bash tool `timeout` to at least `900000` (15 minutes), then poll until it finishes. The default 120 second timeout kills the process during the conversion engine's silent pause and a relaunch starts it over. `--help` and `--list-settings` can stay on the short timeout.
149... 
150... A large source can keep `scai code add` running longer than one `bash` call allows. When
151... the call times out, or returns `Command running in background with ID: <id>` or
152... `Process moved to background with ID: <id>`, the import has not finished and you have no
153... envelope yet. A timeout is neither a failure nor a success.
154... 
155... - **With an id, wait for the real end, in this turn.** Call
156...   `bash_output(bash_id=<id>, wait=true)`, and call it again while it reports running, until
157...   it shows `<status>completed</status>`. Then take its `<exit_code>` and the `--json`
158...   envelope in its `<stdout>`; those are the import's result. Do not end the turn to say it
159...   is still importing: this app does not show the turn cortex starts when the job ends, so
160...   the user would be left with an idle screen. A short line before each wait is fine. Until
161...   you have the result, say only that it is still running,
162...   never that it finished or that nothing is wrong.
163... - **With no id, the run you started has ended or is ending; do not start another.** First
164...   check whether scai is still running with `pgrep -fl '[s]cai code add'` on macOS/Linux, or
165...   `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name LIKE 'scai%' AND CommandLine LIKE '%code add%'"`
166...   on Windows. Output lists a running import;
167...   exit code 1 with no output means no import is running, not that the check failed.
168...   Keep the brackets in `[s]cai`: without them `pgrep -f` matches the shell running the
169...   check and reports an import that has stopped. Run the check as its own command,
170...   never chained with the import, whose text the shell's command line would hold. Repeat it until nothing is running, then treat that run as finished: read any
171...   envelope left in the timed-out output, else run `scai logs --last 5` and read the newest
172...   `scai_error<YYYYMMDD>.log` as below. A logged error is a failure to report.
173...   Start another `scai code add` only when the logs show the first one never ran or was cut
174...   off before it wrote anything, say so to the user first, and launch it with
175...   `run_in_background=true` so you have an id to wait on as above. Two imports writing
176...   `source/` at once corrupt it, and one rerun after a crash only repeats the crash.
177... 
178... **If the import failed** — a non-zero `<exit_code>`, an envelope with `"success": false`,
179... or a job that ended with no envelope at all — find out why before you say anything else:
180... 
181... 1. An envelope with `"success": false` names the cause in `error.code`, `error.message`
182...    and `error.suggestion`. Use those.
183... 2. With no envelope, run `scai logs --last 5`. It prints the log directory (honouring
184...    `SCAI_LOGS_DIR`) and the newest log files on every OS. Read the end of the newest
185...    `scai_error<YYYYMMDD>.log` there for the error code and its message.
186... 3. Tell the user, with the code and message you found (e.g. `CVT0008` or `CRG1001`):
187...    > **The import failed.** `<code>`: `<message>`. `<what you propose next>`.
188... 
189...    Rerunning the same command gives the same failure, so propose a change (the suggestion,
190...    a fix to the files it names) rather than a retry. Do not continue to the next step, and
191...    do not treat the import as done.
192... 
193... **If the failure is `ADD0029` or `CVT0008` with a `Duplicate groups` entry in `error.details`**,
194... the input defines the same object in more than one file and nothing was added. Go to
195... [Duplicated objects](#duplicated-objects). Never add `--keep` or `--dedup keep-first` to get past it
196... on your own.
197... 
198... **If the failure is `ADD0007` after an earlier `scai code add` in this project failed**, and
199... `migration_status` reports no registered code units, the files it lists are most likely what
200... that failed run left in `source/`: a failed add rolls back, but it cannot always remove every
201... file. Keep them. Rerun the same command with `--overwrite` added, which replaces them with this
202... run's output, and tell the user in one line that you are doing so. Never delete files from
203... `source/` or `artifacts/` yourself to clear the way. When the project already has registered
204... units, the files may be code the user added before: ask before you add `--overwrite`.
205... 
206... ### Duplicated objects
207... 
208... `ADD0029` and `CVT0008` carry `error.details["Duplicate groups"]`: per object, its `id`, `database`,
209... `databaseStatus` (`unknown` when the copies collide only because no file named a database) and
210... `copies`, each with `path` (in `source/`), `origin` (`input` or `project`), `inputs` (input file,
211... `database`, `databaseSource`), `contentHash`, `lines` and `differingLines` against the first copy.
212... Classify every group from that evidence and the input layout, then propose one action per group:
213... 
214... | Situation | Evidence | Action |
215... |---|---|---|
216... | S1/S2 different databases | `databaseStatus: unknown`; the copies' input paths sit in different database folders or prefixes, or references name different databases | **Assign databases** (Step 2b) and rerun. Every copy becomes its own unit. |
217... | S3 byte-identical copies | equal `contentHash` | Same database: `code add` already keeps one. Different databases: assign databases; both stay. |
218... | S4 versions of one object in one database | known `database`, or a user-confirmed single database; old script, `_v2`, backup, ALTER script | **Keep one**, chosen by the user: the version deployed on the source when there is a connection (`query_source`), else the user's pick. |
219... | S5 environment copies | database names with environment suffixes, near-identical content | Ask: migrate one environment, or all as separate databases. |
220... | S6 merged or renamed databases | folder and file-prefix databases disagree | Ask which database model is migrated; inside a merged database, S4 applies. |
221... | S8 a later add brings a copy of an object already in the project | `ADD0007` on the registered file, or a copy with `origin: project` | Different database: assign it; it becomes a new unit. Same database: S4. A new copy arranged onto the registered file stops with `ADD0007`: replace it only with the user's consent (`--overwrite`), as the `ADD0007` rule says. A copy under another name keeps the registered one with `--keep source/<path>`. |
222... 
223... 1. Show the user each group in a short table: object, database, each copy's input file, database
224...    and `differingLines`, and your classification.
225... 2. Ask with `ask_user_question`. The options must include **"These are different databases (assign
226...    databases)"** and **"These are environments of one system"**; offer **"Keep one copy"** only for
227...    groups classified S4, naming the copy for each.
228... 3. Apply the answer and rerun the same command:
229...    - assign databases → Step 2b's `--database-map`;
230...    - keep one → `--keep <INPUT_PATH>` per object (the copy's `inputs[].path`, relative to the input
231...      root; `source/<path>` for a copy already in the project). Use `--dedup keep-first` only when
232...      the user explicitly chooses "keep the first file of every object".
233... 4. Report each file in `result.duplicatesSkipped` (`path`, `inputPaths`, `keptPath`,
234...    `keptInputPath`, `policy`) as left out, and `result.decisionRecord`, where the choice is kept.
235... 
236... `ADD0030` means a `--keep` named no copy, two different copies, or would drop a copy the project
237... already registered: show the reason and ask again. A `--keep not applied` entry in `error.details`
238... names a `--keep` that matched no copy while other objects stayed undecided. `ADD0019` / `ADD0021` with `--dedup keep-first`
239... mean no copy can be chosen from the input: tell the user which files to remove.
240... 
241... **When nobody can answer** (an autonomous or headless run, a walker or Hail Mary agent, or no
242... `ask_user_question`): apply only S1 database assignments whose evidence is unambiguous (every
243... folder or prefix matches a database the references or the source name) and S3 identical-copy
244... handling. Never pass `--keep` or `--dedup keep-first`, and never treat an automated reply as the
245... user's choice of a copy. Stop and report the groups still blocked, with their evidence.
246... 
247... ### Step 4: Import ETL
248... 
249... **Skip this entire step for a dbt project.** If Step 1 found `dbt_project.yml`, do **not** ask the
250... ETL question — a dbt workload has no SSIS or Informatica packages, and asking it is a defect. Go
251... straight to Step 5 without calling `ask_user_question`.
252... 
253... ETL belongs in the project from register onward. Read `has_etl_code` from `configure()` (set by
254... `chooseMigrationExtras` or by the parent register skill's extras card). Never ask a standalone ETL
255... yes/no — that question lives only on the extras multi-select.
256... 
257... - If `has_etl_code` is **`false`** (explicitly): the user already said no ETL — proceed to Step 5 without asking.
258... - If `has_etl_code` is **not set**: return to the parent register skill and collect the extras card there, then re-read `has_etl_code`. Do not invent a yes/no.
259... - If `has_etl_code` is **`true`** (explicitly): open [etl.md](etl.md) and follow it. That file holds the ETL import
260...   steps: which directory each platform uses, and how each unit is registered as `kind: etl`. Come
261...   back here at Step 5 when it finishes. Do not register ETL as `customKind`.
262... 
263... ### Step 5: Import Power BI templates
264... 
265... Power BI template (`.pbit`) files are inventory only: `code add` copies them to
266... `source/BI/PowerBI/` and `artifacts/BI/PowerBI/` and never sends them to the conversion engine.
267... Read `has_power_bi` from `configure()`:
268... 
269... - If `has_power_bi` is **`false`**, proceed to Step 6 without asking.
270... - If `has_power_bi` is not set, return to the parent register skill and collect
271...   the extras card, then re-read it.
272... - If `has_power_bi` is **`true`**, first check whether Step 3 already imported
273...   `.pbit` files. If it did, proceed to Step 6. Otherwise ask only for the folder
274...   path and compare it to `<INPUT_PATH>`:
275...   - If it is **the same as, or inside, `<INPUT_PATH>`**, Step 3 already imported it — `code add` claims `.pbit` files anywhere under the input path. Proceed to Step 6 without running a second `code add`.
276...   - Otherwise (a genuinely separate folder) run:
277... 
278... ```bash
279... scai code add -i <POWER_BI_PATH> --json
280... ```
281... 
282... Do **not** pass `--overwrite` here — existing SQL/ETL in `source/` would be wiped. If it
283... times out, runs in the background or fails, handle it as
284... [Step 3](#if-the-import-times-out-or-runs-in-the-background) says.
285... 
286... Confirm files landed in both `source/BI/PowerBI/` and `artifacts/BI/PowerBI/` before continuing.
287... 
288... ### Step 6: Verify Files Were Added
289... 
290... Check that `source/` contains the expected `.sql` files and report a count. Use whichever portable form fits the host:
291... 
292... ```bash
293... # macOS / Linux
294... find source/ -name "*.sql" | head -20
295... find source/ -name "*.sql" | wc -l
296... ```
297... 
298... ```powershell
299... # Windows PowerShell
300... Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.sql source/ | Select-Object -First 20
301... (Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.sql source/).Count
302... ```
303... 
304... ## Output Structure
305... 
306... ```
307... artifacts/source_raw/    Original files copied from input path
308... artifacts/source_split/  sc-tag annotated copies (only created when some file needed tags)
309... source/                  Arranged source files ready for conversion
310... source/_etl/             ETL packages (when present)
311... source/BI/PowerBI/       Power BI `.pbit` templates (inventory only, not converted)
312... artifacts/BI/PowerBI/    Same relative layout as `source/BI/PowerBI/`
313... ```
314... 
315... ## Troubleshooting
316... 
317... | Issue | Solution |
318... |-------|----------|
319... | "conflicting files" error | Use `--overwrite` flag to replace existing files |
320... | `ADD0029` database unknown | The copies collide in `defaultdb`: give the files their databases (Step 2b), see [Duplicated objects](#duplicated-objects) |
321... | `ADD0026` database map rule matches no file | Fix the rule's pattern (relative to the input root) |
322... | `ADD0033` database map rule is shadowed | An earlier rule takes all its files: put the narrower rule first |
323... | `ADD0010: Source files must contain SC tags` | The arrange engine found no `/* <sc-...> */` boundary tags. For a **dbt project**, re-run with `--code-already-split` (required on every dbt add). For a non-dbt source, run Step 2 (`split_code`) first and pass the returned `artifacts/source_split/` path. |
324... | No `.sql` files found after add | Verify input path contains valid SQL files |
325... | Unexpected file arrangement | Check `artifacts/source_raw/` for the original copies |
326... | `split_code` reports verification errors | Manually inspect flagged files; the tool lists each with its boundary and tag counts |
327... 
328... ## CHECKPOINT
329... 
330... Check these yourself against the `--json` envelope. Do **not** turn them into a
331... question — the envelope already says what was imported, and the user cannot
332... verify a count you just computed for them:
333... 
334... - [ ] Every `scai code add` finished with exit code 0 and an envelope with `"success": true`
335...       — a timeout or a background launch is neither; wait for the job as Step 3 says
336... - [ ] `filesCopied` matches the SQL files in the input path
337... - [ ] `.sql` files are present under `source/`
338... - [ ] SQL Server: every file without its own `USE` got a database (Step 2b), or the user chose to
339...       leave the input in one unnamed database
340... - [ ] If Power BI was imported: files exist in both `source/BI/PowerBI/` and `artifacts/BI/PowerBI/`
341... 
342... Stop and ask only when a check fails: say which one, and what you propose to do
343... about it.
344... 
345... ## On Completion
346... 
347... ### Break down `Other` from the registry
348... 
349... `byType` counts units by `objectType`. `Other` is the registry's catch-all, not a type: every
350... type it knows (`trigger`, `index`, `joinIndex`, …) has its own row, so never say a type you
351... expected "lands in" `Other`. Most of its units are missing references — objects the imported
352... code uses but no imported file defines, registered with `isMissing = true`. They count in
353... `codeUnitsAdded`, which is why the total can exceed the objects in the source files.
354... 
355... When `byType` has an `Other` row, look up what is in it before you report, never guess:
356... 
357... ```
358... query_registry(where="source.objectType = 'other' AND isMissing = true", fields="id,source.name,source.schema", limit=5)
359... query_registry(where="source.objectType = 'other' AND NOT isMissing = true", fields="id,source.name,files.source.path", limit=5)
360... ```
361... 
362... Each response's `total` is that group's count; its `results` give a few names to quote. If the
363... two totals do not add up to the `Other` count, give the counts you have and say the rest are
364... unexplained.
365... 
366... ### Report
367... 
368... After the CHECKPOINT passes, tell the user — a statement, not a question. Fill placeholders from the JSON envelope returned by `scai code add --json`.
369... Never report the import as complete, or as fine, without that envelope in hand: on a failure,
370... report it as Step 3 says instead.
371... 
372... > **Import complete.** `<filesCopied>` files imported as `<codeUnitsAdded>` code units, broken down by type (filled from `byType`). Files in `source/`.
373... > *If `byType` has `Other`:* `<missing total>` are missing references: objects your code uses that the imported files do not define (e.g. `<names>`); add their DDL if they belong in the migration. *If the second total is not 0:* `<other total>` more are defined in your files with no type the registry knows (e.g. `<names>`).
374... > *If `etlFilesAdded > 0`:* ETL: `<etlFilesAdded>` files added.
375... > *If `etlFilesSkippedInvalidSchema > 0`:* `<etlFilesSkippedInvalidSchema>` ETL files skipped due to invalid schema.
376... > *If Power BI files were added:* Power BI templates copied to `source/BI/PowerBI/` and `artifacts/BI/PowerBI/` (not converted).
377... > Next, we'll convert these to Snowflake SQL.
378... 
379... Then return to the calling skill **in this same turn**. That last line announces
380... the next step; it is not a stopping point. Under setup, call `progress_setup()`
381... now and start the step it names. Ending the turn on it leaves the user watching
382... an idle screen with nothing to click until they type "continue".

Poll with `bash_output(bash_id=<id>, wait=true)` until `<status>completed</status>`, then read the `--json` envelope — the same wait as [add-code-units](../register-code-units/add-code-units/SKILL.md#if-the-import-times-out-or-runs-in-the-background). `--list-settings` can stay on the short timeout. On a SqlServer full-migration project (`source_language` from `configure()`, compared case-insensitively), append `--generate-source-bindable-format --generate-snowflake-bindable-format`, whatever `subagent_mode` says. They tokenise source (`${name}`) and Snowflake (`<%name%>`) catalog names and write `.scai/bindings/database-bindings.yaml`. Leave them off on a code-conversion-only project, on any other dialect, and on the dbt repointing path — they are invalid alongside `--dbt` and the engine rejects the command (see `dbt/SKILL.md` Step 2). Leaving them off is not an opt-out on a SqlServer full-migration project: `scai code convert` still emits bindable artifacts there, and a stored false is overwritten. Deploy stays legacy-safe: projects converted earlier, with no bindings file, still use `-d snowflake_database`. A convert that wrote an unedited bindings file restores catalog tokens in the SQL on deploy, with or without `-d`. The connection stays on the database passed with `-d` when that flag is set. An edited bindings file requires `--database-bindings` and cannot be combined with `-d`.

214... Only SQL Server's conversion settings define the bindable-format flags today; on every other dialect scai rejects them (`CVT0013`, "Unrecognized option"). If you are unsure whether this dialect supports them, `scai code convert --list-settings --json` lists the settings it accepts. If a convert ever fails with `CVT0013` on one of these flags, rerun without them and do **not** tell the user their scai is outdated or unsupported — the flag is simply not defined for their dialect.

331... ## Understanding EWIs
332... 
333... Reference for answering a question the user asks — not a prompt to go analyze
334... the run. EWIs (Early Warning Issues) indicate conversion items needing attention:
335... 
336... | Severity | Action Required |
337... |----------|----------------|
338... | **Critical** | Must fix before deployment |
339... | **High** | Should fix, may cause runtime errors |
340... | **Medium** | Review recommended |
341... | **Low** | Minor issues, optional fixes |
342... 
343... **Common EWI codes:**
344... - `SSC-EWI-0030`: Dynamic SQL (requires manual review)
345... - `SSC-FDM-*`: Functional differences (behavior may differ)
346... - `SSC-PRF-*`: Performance remarks (optimization suggested)

messages.text:
For key-pair auth, I'd generate an RSA key pair using openssl, but I need to think through the passphrase issue — an encrypted private key needs a passphrase that's really a secret I shouldn't be handling myself, so I should prefer an unencrypted key for automation purposes despite the security tradeoff.

Given this will run unattended, I'll generate an unencrypted private key with restricted file permissions and be upfront about that tradeoff rather than asking another question. There's a chicken-and-egg problem though: since the connection is already dead, the user has to add the public key via ALTER USER themselves in Snowsight using their own MFA login — so I'll request they run that exact statement, then point the connection config at the generated private key path.

Generating the key pair now.

Key-pair it is. I'll generate the key pair locally, then you'll add the public key in Snowsight — that's the one step only you can do, since the CLI login is what's broken and your browser session has MFA.

I'm generating the private key without a passphrase, because AIM logs in unattended and there'd be nothing to type a passphrase into. It'll be locked to your user with `600` permissions. Say so if you'd rather have an encrypted key.

A child process running only a connections-list command fails before even executing, meaning startup authentication itself is broken — the agent runtime must be authenticating to Snowflake at spawn using stale config. I'm trying to figure out why my own session still works: it seems my session authenticated earlier and is tied to a different account than the one now failing.

Children try to establish inference via the active connection, which has key-pair auth set up, yet still report MFA — probably the spawn path isn't reading the authenticator/private_key_file settings or is caching old credentials. Since the migration's target connection is actually fixed and verified, and the only remaining issue is the subagent runtime not picking up the new config, I think the cheapest fix to test is restarting the app so children inherit the updated credentials — otherwise I can just run the assessment serially myself in this session. I want to present this clearly to the user without overstating certainty, since I've only confirmed where the failure occurs, not the exact root cause.

That settles it. A child that only runs `cortex connections list` — no `configure`, no Snowflake work of its own — still dies in one second with the same MFA error. So the failure is in how child processes authenticate at spawn, not in your migration's connection.

Here's what I've actually verified:

- Your project's target connection now logs in with key-pair auth. `configure()` succeeded, and AIM created its tracking database.
- The parent session is healthy: docs search and `scai assessment object-exclusion` both work.
- Every child process fails at startup regardless of what I ask it to do.

What I haven't confirmed is why. The most likely explanation is simply ordering: the app launched while `config.toml` still held the password, and child processes are being spawned from that stale credential. I can't test a restart from in here.

That leaves two ways forward, and the assessment doesn't depend on subagents working — the analysis commands run locally.

103... ### 1. Generate
104... 
105... ```bash
106... # Project mode (preferred)
107... scai assessment sql-dynamic generate \
108...   --project-dir <project_dir> \

118... **What this creates:**
119... - A JSON file with `metadata` (totals, generation timestamp, input files) and a `codeUnits` map.
120... - Each code unit holds `codeUnitId`, `procedureName`, `fileName`, `codeUnitStartLine`, `linesOfCode`, the full `procedure` text, and an `occurrences` list.
121... - Each occurrence starts with `status: PENDING` and empty analysis fields, ready for review. Its `issueCode` names the code that reported it.
122... 
123... ### 2. View occurrences for a code unit
124... 
125... Group occurrences by file or by code unit:
126... 
127... ```bash
128... # All occurrences in the file containing a given record (or with no --id, list all files)
129... scai assessment sql-dynamic show-file <analysis.json>
130... scai assessment sql-dynamic show-file <analysis.json> --filename <fileName>

136... scai assessment sql-dynamic show <analysis.json> --id <N>
137... ```
138... 
139... **Analysis approach:**
140... 1. Use `show-file` to enumerate code units per file.
141... 2. Pick one code unit and read its full procedure source (`show-code-unit`).
142... 3. Open the dialect-appropriate `reference/PATTERNS_<DIALECT>.md` and classify each dynamic SQL site against the catalog.
143... 4. Update each occurrence individually (next step).
144... 5. Move on to the next code unit.
145... 
146... ### 3. Classify patterns
147... 
148... **Reference per dialect (must read before classifying):**
149... - **SQL Server migrations** → `reference/PATTERNS_TRANSACT.md`
150... - **Redshift migrations** → `reference/PATTERNS_REDSHIFT.md`
151... - **Oracle migrations** → `reference/PATTERNS_ORACLE.md`
152... - **Teradata migrations** → `reference/PATTERNS_TERADATA.md`
153... 
154... ⚠️ Pick the correct catalog based on the source platform (see [Source Platform Detection](#source-platform-detection)).
155... 
156... **Process:**
157... 1. Read every pattern in the appropriate catalog before reviewing the first occurrence.
158... 2. Compare the procedure source against each pattern.
159... 3. Identify all patterns that apply (multiple may apply to the same occurrence).
160... 4. Collect the analysis fields described below.
161... 5. Pass the patterns to `--category` as a pipe-separated string (`"Pattern-A | Pattern-B"`); SCAI stores them as a list.
162... 
163... **Per-occurrence fields to collect:**
164... 
165... **generated_sql (`--generated-sql`):**
166... - The actual SQL that would be executed at runtime.
167... - Include the dynamic-SQL construction logic so it is clear what is built.
168... - Use representative values for variables; provide a complete best-effort statement (no ellipses or vague placeholders).
169... 
170... **sql_classification (`--sql-classification`):**
171... - DQL (SELECT) | DML (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) | DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP) | DCL (GRANT/REVOKE) | TCL (COMMIT/ROLLBACK) | UNKNOWN.
172... - Drives operation-level prioritization. **Pattern tagging is separate** — do not infer patterns from the SQL classification; choose them from the dialect catalog and pass via `--category`.
173... 
174... **notes (`--notes`):** A JSON object with three required keys (see [Notes Structure](#notes-structure)).
175... 
176... ### 4. Score complexity
177... 
178... **Scale:** `low` (0–30), `medium` (31–60), `high` (61–85), `critical` (86–100).
179... 
180... **Process:**
181... 1. Start from the base complexity of the matched pattern in `PATTERNS_<DIALECT>.md`.
182... 2. Read the actual code carefully.
183... 3. Override the base score **only if** the code materially differs from the pattern baseline.
184... 4. Document the override reasoning under `complexity` in the notes JSON.
185... 
186... ### 5. Update an occurrence
187... 
188... ```bash
189... scai assessment sql-dynamic update <analysis.json> \
190...   --id <N> \
191...   --line <line_number> \
192...   --status REVIEWED \
193...   --category "Pattern-Name | Additional-Pattern" \
194...   --complexity medium \
195...   --sql-classification DDL \
196...   --generated-sql "CREATE TABLE dbo.TempTable (ID INT, Name VARCHAR(100))" \
197...   --notes '{
198...     "justification": "Line X uses dynamic SQL to construct a table name from user-supplied variables...",
199...     "complexity": "- Deep concatenation chains (5+ levels)\n- No input validation detected\n- Cross-schema dynamic references",
200...     "migration_considerations": "- Recommend Snowflake IDENTIFIER() function\n- Add input validation before migration\n- Estimated effort: 4–6 hours per occurrence"
201...   }'
202... ```
203... 
204... **Command notes:**
205... - The first positional argument is the analysis JSON path.
206... - `--id` is required; it identifies the occurrence to update.
207... - `--line` should be set after reading the procedure source — generated records start with `line = 0`. Keep `0` only when the source line cannot be reliably determined.
208... - At least one of `--line`, `--status`, `--category`, `--complexity`, `--notes`, `--generated-sql`, `--sql-classification` must be supplied.
209... - `--category` accepts pipe-separated names; SCAI splits them into a list internally.
210... 
211... ### 6. Track progress
212... 
213... ```bash
214... scai assessment sql-dynamic stats <analysis.json>
215... ```
216... 
217... Reports totals, per-status counts, and per-category counts. Repeat steps 2–5 until no `PENDING` records remain.
218... 
219... ## Notes Structure
220... 
221... Each `--notes` value must be a JSON object with the three required keys below:
222... 
223... ```json
224... {
225...   "justification": "Why this is dynamic SQL, what it does, context.",
226...   "complexity": "Technical factors affecting migration difficulty.",
227...   "migration_considerations": "Snowflake-specific recommendations, alternatives, effort estimate."
228... }
229... ```
230... 
231... **Field length and tone:**
232... - `justification`: 40+ words, full sentences, reference specific code elements.
233... - `complexity`: 30+ words, full sentences, list the technical drivers.
234... - `migration_considerations`: 40+ words, full sentences, end with a concrete effort estimate.
235... - Do **not** write "similar to occurrence ##"; restate the context explicitly for every record.
236... 
237... **Formatting tips:**
238... - Use `\n` for line breaks within a multi-line field.
239... - Single-quote the entire JSON in shell to avoid quote escaping headaches.
240... 
241... ## Reference Files
242... 
243... - `reference/PATTERNS_TRANSACT.md` — pattern catalog for SQL Server → Snowflake migrations.
244... - `reference/PATTERNS_REDSHIFT.md` — pattern catalog for Redshift → Snowflake migrations.
245... - `reference/PATTERNS_ORACLE.md` — pattern catalog for Oracle → Snowflake migrations.
246... - `reference/PATTERNS_TERADATA.md` — pattern catalog for Teradata → Snowflake migrations.
247...

249... - Use `PATTERNS_TRANSACT.md` for SQL Server sources.

481... ## 12. Template/Token Replacement
482... 
483... **Risk Level:** MEDIUM-HIGH (65/100)
484... 
485... **Description:** SQL is built from a template by replacing tokens (macros/placeholders) such as `{WHERE}`, `<<Schema>>`, `@TOKEN@`, or `/*PLACEHOLDER*/`.
486... 
487... **Characteristics:**
488... - Uses `REPLACE()` / `STUFF()` / `FORMATMESSAGE()` or custom string functions to inject fragments
489... - Template may come from a config table or be composed across multiple variables
490... - Can hide whether the replacement is a **value** (unsafe) or an **identifier** (needs whitelist)
491... 
492... **Example:**
493... ```sql
494... DECLARE @template NVARCHAR(MAX) = N'SELECT * FROM dbo.Orders WHERE /*FILTER*/'
495... DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) = REPLACE(@template, '/*FILTER*/', N'Status = @Status')
496... EXEC sp_executesql @sql, N'@Status NVARCHAR(50)', @Status = @Status
497... ```

I'm classifying both occurrences in usp_ProcessBudgetConsolidation as SSC-EWI-0125. The first is the dynamic SQL construction using REPLACE to swap in literal fragments like the ConsolidatedAmount filter condition, which fits a template/token-replacement, parameter-driven pattern.

For id 1 (the build/REPLACE at line 378), I'm scoring it as Template/Token-Replacement with Clause-Assembly and Unsafe-Value-Concatenation, since @RoundingPrecision gets CAST and concatenated into the statement — a potential injection surface, though its XML-sourced INT typing limits real risk. Base complexity around 65 pushes it into the "high" band given the temp-table reference inside the dynamic SQL too.

For id 2 (the sp_executesql call at line 413), it's primarily Parameter-Driven with a low base score, but the OUTPUT parameter and the #temp table scope dependency — which Snowflake Scripting handles differently — justify bumping it up to medium.

Both occurrences sit in `usp_ProcessBudgetConsolidation`: one builds the statement by token-replacing fragments of a SQL template, the other executes it with an OUTPUT parameter against a temp table. Recording each separately.

input.content:
# Workload context

## At a glance

This is a single-schema SQL Server financial planning workload: one database
(`FINANCIAL_PLANNING`), one business schema (`Planning`), and 26 reachable code
units out of 45 registered. It holds 8 tables, 2 views, 4 functions, 6 stored
procedures and 3 user-defined table types, plus 13 indexes that have no
Snowflake counterpart. There is no ETL tool, no BI layer and no scheduler in the
drop, so the lineage graph names no source system and no reporting target: all
48 graph nodes and 96 edges are internal to this schema. Everything the code
does is budget planning, consolidation, allocation and period-end close.

## Subject areas

### Budget master data and structure

The reference and transactional backbone, all under
`source/financial_planning/planning/table/`. `GLAccount`, `CostCenter` and
`FiscalPeriod` are the dimensions; `BudgetHeader` and `BudgetLineItem` hold
budget versions and their amounts. `CostCenter` is a self-referencing hierarchy,
which is why so much of the logic in this workload is recursive.
`BudgetHeader` carries a self-reference too (`BaseBudgetHeaderID`), so budget
versions are chained to a base version. `BudgetHeader.ExtendedProperties` is an
`XML` column with two XML indexes over it
(`source/financial_planning/planning/table/budgetheader.sql`, and the two index
files split out during import).

### Cost centre hierarchy navigation

Three objects exist only to walk the `CostCenter` tree:
`fn_GetHierarchyPath` builds a delimited ancestor path for one cost centre
(`function/fn_gethierarchypath.sql`), `tvf_ExplodeCostCenterHierarchy` expands a
subtree to a row set with a depth limit and an as-of date
(`function/tvf_explodecostcenterhierarchy.sql`), and
`fn_GetAllocationFactor` computes an allocation weight between a source and a
target cost centre for a given basis and period
(`function/fn_getallocationfactor.sql`). All three are read by the procedures
rather than by anything outside the schema. `fn_GetHierarchyPath` is one of the
anchor objects the scan found, because nothing in the drop writes to it and it
reads tables — it is a sink in graph terms, not a business outcome.

### Budget consolidation

`usp_ProcessBudgetConsolidation` (`procedure/usp_processbudgetconsolidation.sql`,
554 lines, the largest unit) rolls budget line items up the cost centre
hierarchy, applies eliminations, and writes consolidated amounts and journal
entries. It reads `vw_BudgetConsolidationSummary`, uses both hierarchy
functions, and is the only unit in the workload containing dynamic SQL. Its
header records that the imported definition is the effective one after four
SQL Server patches, and that a test-only XML hook was excluded from this drop.

### Cost allocation

`usp_ExecuteCostAllocation` (`procedure/usp_executecostallocation.sql`) performs
step-down allocation driven by rules in `AllocationRule`, resolved through
`vw_AllocationRuleTargets`, weighting with `fn_GetAllocationFactor`. The
allocation targets are stored as XML inside `AllocationRule` and parsed by the
view. The procedure serialises itself with `sp_getapplock`/`sp_releaseapplock`
and throttles with `WAITFOR DELAY`, so it was written to be run concurrently
with other work on a shared instance.

### Intercompany reconciliation

`usp_ReconcileIntercompanyBalances`
(`procedure/usp_reconcileintercompanybalances.sql`) matches balances between
entity pairs across `ConsolidationJournal` / `ConsolidationJournalLine`, hashes
rows with `HASHBYTES` to detect differences, and builds an XML report using
`sp_xml_preparedocument` plus `OPENXML`. This is the only unit that produces
something report-shaped, but the result is returned to the caller rather than
written to a table or a file, so the scan recorded no report anchor for it.

### Forecasting

`usp_GenerateRollingForecast` (`procedure/usp_generaterollingforecast.sql`)
projects a rolling forecast using window functions, `PERCENTILE_CONT`, and a
dynamic `PIVOT` whose column list is assembled with `FOR XML PATH`. It reads
`tvf_GetBudgetVariance`, the other anchor object, which compares a base budget
version against a comparison version.

### Period-end close orchestration

`usp_PerformFinancialClose` (`procedure/usp_performfinancialclose.sql`) is the
top of the call tree: its header states it depends on every table, view and
function in the schema, and it calls `usp_ProcessBudgetConsolidation`,
`usp_ExecuteCostAllocation` and `usp_ReconcileIntercompanyBalances` in turn with
OUTPUT parameters. This is the closest thing in the drop to a business process
boundary, and it is the natural root of the dependency order.

## Pipelines and schedules

No scheduler artefact is present. The only orchestration visible in the code is
procedural: `usp_PerformFinancialClose` calling the three worker procedures,
each of which logs its steps into a local table variable rather than a
persistent run table. `usp_BulkImportBudgetData`
(`procedure/usp_bulkimportbudgetdata.sql`) is the single entry point for data
arriving from outside, via `BULK INSERT` with a format file and an
`OPENQUERY`/`OPENROWSET` path for ad-hoc file access; the file locations and the
cadence are not stated. There is no calendar table driving execution —
`FiscalPeriod` defines accounting periods, not run times.

## Where data leaves

Nothing in this drop writes outside the `Planning` schema. The scan found zero
exit jobs, zero reports, zero file targets and zero external database targets.
Two candidate outcomes are returned to the caller rather than persisted: the
reconciliation XML from `usp_ReconcileIntercompanyBalances` and the forecast
result set from `usp_GenerateRollingForecast`. Whoever consumes them is not
stated. The `OPENQUERY` reference in the import procedure points at a linked
server, so there is at least one external system on the inbound side, but it is
not named in the code.

## Scratch, sandbox and personal areas

None. Object exclusion analysed 45 objects and found no temporary, staging,
deprecated, test or duplicate objects, and no version conflicts. The folder
layout is by object type only, with no per-person or per-environment areas.
Three registry entries under `Other` are parser artefacts rather than real
objects: a `CROSS APPLY` alias (`ca`), a temp table (`#MergeOutput`) and
`OPENXML`, all arising from procedure bodies. Two of these were nevertheless
picked up as write-only anchors by the scan and should not be treated as
business outcomes.

## What the code cannot show

- **No consumer for any result.** With no BI layer, no scheduler export and no
  query logs provided, nothing confirms that any of these outputs is still used,
  or by whom. This affects every subject area, and it is the reason the use case
  catalogue here rests on code structure rather than on evidence of use. The
  user was offered a query-log usage summary and Extended Events discovery and
  declined both for this run.
- **No inbound source identified.** `usp_BulkImportBudgetData` loads from files
  and a linked server, but neither the file producer nor the linked server is
  named, so the upstream of the whole workload is unknown.
- **No run cadence.** Whether the close runs monthly, quarterly or on demand is
  not stated anywhere in the code, which matters for sizing the migrated
  workload and for choosing between a Task schedule and on-demand execution.
- **Actuals are absent.** `tvf_GetBudgetVariance` compares two budget versions,
  not budget against actuals, despite its name; no actuals table exists in the
  drop. If variance against actuals is a real requirement, the table holding
  actuals was not included.

messages.text:
The assessment is complete. Here's what it found.

**Your workload** is one SQL Server database (`FINANCIAL_PLANNING`), one schema, 45 registered objects of which 32 are deployable: 8 tables, 2 views, 4 functions, 6 procedures, 3 table types. No ETL, no BI, no scratch or test objects — object exclusion found nothing excludable. Estimated effort came out at 14.8 hours.

**Two business use cases**, both rated low confidence — honestly so, because you declined query logs and Extended Events, and the code contains no scheduler, no BI layer and nothing that writes outside its own schema. Nothing in the drop proves these outputs are still consumed. The plan is three waves: cost centre hierarchy navigation (3 objects), then budget consolidation and period-end close (26 objects), then 5 data-only objects.

**The hard parts are concentrated, not spread out.** 83 EWIs over 37 distinct kinds, and the shape matters more than the count:

- **XML is the dominant theme.** `BudgetHeader.ExtendedProperties` is an XML column; `vw_AllocationRuleTargets` parses XML with `.value()`, `.nodes()`, `.exist()` and `.query()`, none of which exist in Snowflake; `usp_ReconcileIntercompanyBalances` uses `sp_xml_preparedocument` plus `OPENXML`, which has no equivalent at all. All of it needs rewriting onto `PARSE_XML`, `XMLGET` and `LATERAL FLATTEN`.
- **Transaction control won't survive as written.** Savepoints, `XACT_ABORT`, `@@TRANCOUNT` and `XACT_STATE()` comparisons have no counterparts. One flagged branch is already unreachable: `XACT_STATE() = -1` can never be true in Snowflake.
- **Row-at-a-time logic throughout.** Recursive scalar functions, updatable cursors with `FOR UPDATE`, a multi-statement table function that no function body was generated for, plus `sp_getapplock` and `WAITFOR DELAY` that exist only to protect a shared server.
- **One genuine correctness risk:** `SSC-EWI-TS0082` converted a `CROSS APPLY` to a `LEFT OUTER JOIN`. Those aren't equivalent — the converted view can return more rows than the source. That one needs validating rather than reviewing.
- **17 instances of `SSC-EWI-0108`** are subqueries Snowflake will reject at compile time, not behaviour differences.

Each of the 37 issue types now has a researched problem description and a concrete fix in the report, and both dynamic SQL occurrences in `usp_ProcessBudgetConsolidation` are reviewed individually.

Two things to flag plainly. Your Snowflake connection was rejecting logins because MFA is required on that account; it now uses key-pair auth, and the private key at `~/.snowflake/keys/aim_financial_planning_key.p8` is the only copy — losing it means redoing that setup. Separately, subagents in this session still can't authenticate at spawn, so I ran all six analyses serially here instead of in parallel; the output is the same, and restarting the app will likely clear it.

The report is at `assessment/aim_workspace_migration_plan_20261122_013010.html`, with a PDF alongside it.

The converted files ended up in the snowflake/ directory within the project.

Your converted Snowflake SQL is under the project's `snowflake/` directory:

`/Users/lakshmi/Projects/snowflake-migration/aim-workspace/snowflake/`

It mirrors the source layout, organised by database, schema and object type — for example:

- `snowflake/financial_planning/planning/procedure/usp_processbudgetconsolidation.sql`
- `snowflake/financial_planning/planning/view/vw_allocationruletargets.sql`
- `snowflake/financial_planning/planning/function/fn_gethierarchypath.sql`
- `snowflake/financial_planning/planning/table/budgetheader.sql`

Two related locations, since they come up often:

- `source/` holds the arranged original T-SQL, one object per file, which is what the converter read.
- `assessment/` holds the report and the PDF.

One thing worth knowing about the converted files: unresolved issues are marked inline in them, so you can find the work by searching rather than cross-referencing the report. Blocking ones appear as `!!!RESOLVE EWI!!!` with the code and message next to them, and advisory ones as `SSC-FDM-` comments. For example, `grep -rn "RESOLVE EWI" snowflake/` lists every site that won't deploy as written.

Also note the converted SQL carries catalog placeholders like `<%financial_planning%>` rather than hard-coded database names — those are substituted at deploy time from `.scai/bindings/database-bindings.yaml`, so leave them in place.

# Configure sandbox profile

For non-Snowflake sources: the sandbox profile (`--profile`) and database
bindings deploy/migrate/validate run on.

## Step 1: Explain what this step configures

In a sentence or two of your own, tell the user what the **sandbox profile** is: the source and Snowflake connections and database bindings (source → Snowflake databases) every deploy/migrate/validate/test run uses, so they hit a sandbox, not production. They confirm it before saving and can change it in Settings.

A source connection is **required**, even for synthetic test data:
deploy, migrate and validate read from it. Say so if asked to skip it,
unless `configure()` shows `migration_scope: deploy_only` (Deploy-only).
`no-source-project.md` overrides Steps 3-6.

A profile names its bindings file (`--database-bindings`); editing one
changes every profile using it. A profile for some databases binds a copy
keeping their code's tokens. A run's scope isn't a profile's.

## Step 2: Choose the sandbox profile name

Ask via `ask_user_question` (`multiSelect = false`) to use `sandbox` or type
another name. Read `configure()` first: ask any Step 3 connection question in
this same card.

If `.scai/config/profiles.local.yaml` has this name, ask whether to replace
it (in Step 6) or pick another.

## Step 3: Resolve source and target connections

Call `configure()` and read `source_connection` and `snowflake_connection`.

Show this **verbatim** first, asked anything or not:

> **Use a non-production instance.** Connect to a dev, test, or sandbox
> database — not production. Migration operations can introduce significant
> query load, long-running reads, and potential locking on the source database
> during data migration and validation phases.

**Both already set:** do **not** ask about either connection here. Say the
sandbox will use **Source:** `<source_connection>` and **Snowflake:**
`<snowflake_connection>`, confirmed before saving, then go on to Step 4.

**One or both missing:** ask only for the missing ones, one question each
(`multiSelect = false`), in the Step 2 card:

1. **Source connection** — existing source connections for this dialect.
   Always include **Create a new connection** last. **Never** offer "no
   source connection", "synthetic only", or "skip".
2. **Target Snowflake connection** — existing Snowflake connections, a
   `last_used_snowflake_connection:` first as `<name> (recommended)`,
   description "Last used": only a recommendation, so save nothing until
   the user picks. Always include **Create a new connection** last.

On **Create a new connection**, load its skill (source: the dialect's, as
mapped in `configure-source-connection.md`; Snowflake:
`../connection/snowflake-connection/SKILL.md`), then re-read `configure()`
and re-ask.

No source connection yet: stop until there is one.

## Step 4: Bind each source database the code covers

Bind exactly the source databases the registered code lives in. Never list
the connection's databases, run a catalog query, or ask which are in scope: a
database with no registered code is never offered and never bound.

One source connection covers every database here: never ask for, or create,
a connection or profile per database.

Call `list_source_databases()`; if it fails, stop. Nothing registered: stop.
Tell the user to add or extract code first. Each entry's `token` keys the
bindings file. A `placeholder` entry (`defaultdb`, `database_unspecified`)
or `unitsWithoutDatabase` is code with no database part: bind it to the
source connection's default database (`scai connection list -l <dialect>
--json`) and show it in the Step 6 recap.

Suggest a target per database: its `configure()` `snowflake_targets:` entry,
else `snowflake_database:` for the first, else the entry's `suggestedTarget`
(an unbound placeholder has none: the default database's name).
When the result has `databasePrefix` (a shared account), every target,
suggested or typed, must start with it: prepend it to any that doesn't.
Then one `ask_user_question` with one question per database with code
(`multiSelect = false`), headed by the source database: suggested target
labelled **(recommended)**; freeform override allowed. Reject duplicate
targets; re-ask on conflict.

## Step 5: Check the target DBs

For each target, run `SHOW DATABASES LIKE '<TARGET>'`. It exists only if a
returned `name` equals it exactly (upper-cased if unquoted): `LIKE` ignores
case and `_` is a wildcard. Create nothing yet: missing ones go to the
recap. If the check fails, stop with remediation.

For existing targets, call
`configure(check_target_tables="<token>=<TARGET>,…", check_target_connection="<snowflake>")`
and carry each `target_database_exists:` line to the recap: what deploy
replaces there. On `unavailable: …`, say the check didn't run. Any
target missing: add `check_create_database=true`.

## Step 6: Confirm, persist, and complete

Show a recap (name, description, source connection, Snowflake connection,
bindings file, each source database and its target, targets to create,
warning on `create_database: denied` here and on the save option), and
each `target_database_exists:` line that replaces something, adding "_Deploy
overwrites these objects; their code and rows will be lost._"

Per existing target deploy replaces something in, or whose check couldn't
run, ask a separate yes/no naming the database and what deploy replaces:
**Replace these objects in <DB>** /
**Pick another target** (back to Step 4). Never answer it yourself: with no
person to answer, stop and escalate it.

Then ask **Yes, save profile** / **Change something**. On
**Change something**, ask what to change; for a connection, ask the Step 3
question for that connection (the current one first, labelled **current**,
**Create a new connection** last), then show the recap again. Re-run Step 5
after changing the Snowflake connection or a mapping. Only after Yes:

1. Create no database: item 5 creates each missing target from its
   converted DDL, collation included. On a
   `target_database_status_<db>: error`, stop with its remediation.

2. Write `.scai/bindings/database-bindings.yaml` (convert generates it);
   both maps key on convert's token:

   ```yaml
   source:
     <token>: <SOURCE_DB>
   snow:
     <token>: <TARGET_DB>
   ```

   AIM reads only this file, so every profile points at it: edit it in
   place. Per database with code keep its `source:` entry (a
   placeholder's is the connection's default) and set `snow:` to the
   confirmed target. Drop `source:` and `snow:` entries for databases with
   no registered code only after the Step 4 inventory is complete; else keep
   them all. Never replace the file with a source→target-only list, or
   drop a database with code to fit one profile.

3. Create the profile:

```bash
scai profile create <name> \
  --source-connection <source> \
  --snowflake-connection <snowflake> \
  --database-bindings .scai/bindings/database-bindings.yaml \
  --sandbox \
  --description "Sandbox profile for <project-name>: AIM's deploy, migrate, validate and test connections."
```

To replace a name, `scai profile remove <name>` first.

4. `scai profile set-default <name>`

5. Persist profile **and** connections, never `snowflake_database`
   (the bindings file holds the targets):

```
configure(sandbox_profile="<name>", source_connection="<source>",
  snowflake_connection="<snowflake>", ensure_target_database=true)
```

## Deploy-only

`migration_scope: deploy_only` has no source database; the profile is
Snowflake-only. The steps above change:

- Steps 1 and 3: leave the source out; ask only for Snowflake.
- Step 4: bind as usual. Keep each `source:` entry convert wrote; a
  placeholder binds to its own name.
- Step 6: omit `--source-connection` from `scai profile create` and
  `source_connection` from `configure`.

messages.text:
The user's asking about the source connection, so I should explain why it's needed—deploy, migrate, and validate steps all read from it, and equivalence testing needs it to capture baselines—and then list what details I'd need: host/port, database name, and authentication method (SQL auth or Windows/Entra).

If they don't have a SQL Server instance available at all, the honest alternative is deploy_only scope, which skips testing and data migration and keeps the project in manual run mode. I should lay out both paths clearly and let them choose.

Happy to explain.

**What the source connection is for.** Three later steps read from your SQL Server, which is why it's required rather than optional:

- **Equivalence testing** — the way AIM proves a converted procedure behaves the same is to run the original on SQL Server, run the converted one on Snowflake, and compare. Without the source there's nothing to compare against.
- **Data migration** — moving the rows out of your tables.
- **Data validation** — comparing source and Snowflake row counts, checksums or rows after the move.

Deploying the converted DDL to Snowflake does not itself need it. So the question is really which of those three you intend to do.

**What I'd need from you.** The server host and port, the database name (`FINANCIAL_PLANNING`), the authentication method, and the login. The password is never typed in chat — I'd ask for it in a masked field that stores it securely and never shows me the value.

**The important caveat:** point this at a dev, test or restored-backup instance. Data migration and validation put real load on the source — long-running reads and potential locking.

**If you don't have a SQL Server instance available**, that's a legitimate position, and there's a supported mode for it: deploy-only. It converts and deploys to Snowflake, and skips testing, data migration and validation entirely. You'd be trusting the conversion without equivalence proof — which, given what this assessment found (XML rewrites, transaction control with no counterpart, a `CROSS APPLY` that may now return extra rows), I'd be reluctant to recommend for these six procedures. But it's a real option if the source is genuinely unreachable.

1... ---
2... name: sql-server-connection
3... description: Connect to a source SQL Server database for migration to Snowflake using scai CLI. Triggers: sql server, sqlserver, source connection, source database, connect to sql server, add sql server connection, windows authentication, integrated security, kerberos.
4... license: Proprietary. See License-Skills for complete terms
5... ---
6... 
7... # SQL Server Connection Skill
8... 
9... ## On Entry
10... 
11... Tell the user:
12... > **Setting up SQL Server connection** — I'll configure and test a connection to your source SQL Server database. I'll need some connection details from you shortly.
13... 
14... ## Prerequisites
15... 
16... - Network access to the SQL Server instance
17... - SQL Server credentials (username/password for Standard auth, or domain credentials for Windows auth)
18... - The `scai` CLI installed and available
19... 
20... ## Required Connection Details
21... 
22... | Parameter | Required | Description |
23... |-----------|----------|-------------|
24... | `-s, --source-connection` | Yes | Friendly name for this connection |
25... | `--auth` | Yes | Authentication method: `standard` or `windows` |
26... | `--server-url` | Yes | SQL Server hostname or IP |
27... | `--database` | Yes | Default database; the connection still reaches every database on the server |
28... | `--user` | For standard auth | SQL Server username |
29... | `--password` | For standard auth | SQL Server password (prompted securely) |
30... | `--port` | No | Port number (default: 1433) |
31... | `--trust-server-certificate` | No | Trust server certificate |
32... | `--encrypt` | No | Encrypt connection |
33... | `kerberos_principal` | SPCS Windows auth | Client principal (`client@REALM`) written on the profile after `add-sql-server`. Not a SQL username. |
34... 
35... ### One connection covers every database on the server
36... 
37... `--database` is only the connection's default. Extraction reaches the server's other databases with `-d` (`scai code extract -s <NAME> -d A,B`, see `../../register-code-units/extract-code-units/SKILL.md`), and deploy, migrate and validate find each object's database through the project's database bindings.
38... 
39... - **Never** create one connection per database: a project spanning several databases on one server uses one connection.
40... - **Never** point the connection at `master` or another system database to "cover" several; pick a user database the project migrates.
41... - "A connection with both databases" (or several) means one connection whose default is one of them, then extracting with `-d A,B`. Tell the user so.
42... 
43... ## Workflow
44... 
45... ### Step 1: Ask which authentication the server accepts
46... 
47... Skip this question when the user already said Windows authentication is required; go to Step 1b. Skip it when they already said SQL authentication; go to Step 1c.
48... 
49... Ask the user:
50... 
51... > How should I sign in to this SQL Server?
52... > 1. SQL authentication — username and password
53... > 2. Windows authentication — a domain account, no SQL login
54... 
55... **Wait for the user's response — do not proceed until they choose.**
56... 
57... | Answer | Action |
58... |--------|--------|
59... | SQL authentication | Step 1c, then Step 2 |
60... | Windows authentication | Step 1b |
61... 
62... ### Step 1b: Where the worker runs
63... 
64... Ask the user:
65... 
66... > Windows authentication uses the account that is already signed in when the worker runs on a domain-joined Windows machine. On Snowpark Container Services the worker is Linux, so it needs a Kerberos keytab. Where will the Data Exchange Worker run?
67... > 1. On a domain-joined Windows machine
68... > 2. On Snowpark Container Services
69... 
70... **Wait for the user's response — do not proceed until they choose.**
71... 
72... | Answer | Action |
73... |--------|--------|
74... | Domain-joined Windows machine | Step 3 (Windows on this host), then Step 4. When this session is WSL or Linux, follow `./references/wsl-windows-auth.md` before Step 4. |
75... | Snowpark Container Services | Read [`../../data-infrastructure/references/sqlserver-spcs-windows-auth.md`](../../data-infrastructure/references/sqlserver-spcs-windows-auth.md) and complete only **Save the source connection**. Then Step 4. |
76... 
77... ### Step 1c: Ask how to provide SQL credentials
78... 
79... Ask the user:
80... 
81... > I need the following to connect to SQL Server:
82... > - **Server URL** (hostname or IP)
83... > - **Default database** (a user database, not `master`; the connection still reaches the server's other databases)
84... > - **Username** and **Password**
85... >
86... > How would you like to provide these?
87... 
88... Options:
89... 1. **1Password** - Credentials stored in 1Password vault
90... 2. **Enter manually** - Provide values interactively
91... 
92... ### Step 2: Route Based on Answer
93... 
94... | User says | Action |
95... |-----------|--------|
96... | "1Password" | Follow `../1PASSWORD.md` |
97... | "Enter manually" | Proceed to Step 3 (manual entry) |
98... | Other credential manager | Check if `../references/<NAME>.md` exists; if not, ask user to explain their setup |
99... 
100... ### Step 3: Add the Connection
101... 
102... **SQL authentication, interactive:**
103... ```bash
104... scai connection add-sql-server
105... ```
106... 
107... Enter the password only at the CLI's hidden prompt. If a CI runner already
108... injects it through a named environment variable, keep the command text opaque:
109... reference the variable (for example, `--password "$PASSWORD_ENV_VAR"`), never
110... copy its value into the command. Inspect variable names only; never print the
111... environment or the variable's value.
112... 
113... **SQL authentication, inline.** Password is prompted securely. Use the port
114... the user supplied (`--port`); do not assume 1433 when they named a different
115... one.
116... ```bash
117... scai connection add-sql-server \
118...   -s <SOURCE_CONNECTION_NAME> \
119...   --auth standard \
120...   --server-url <SERVER_URL> \
121...   --port <PORT> \
122...   --database <DATABASE> \
123...   --user <USERNAME> \
124...   --trust-server-certificate
125... ```
126... 
127... **Windows authentication on this host.** No username and no password:
128... ```bash
129... scai connection add-sql-server \
130...   -s <SOURCE_CONNECTION_NAME> \
131...   --auth windows \
132...   --server-url <SERVER_URL> \
133...   --port 1433 \
134...   --database <DATABASE>
135... ```
136... 
137... Snowpark Container Services Windows authentication is added from the reference in Step 1b. Do not add it again here.
138... 
139... **Correcting a saved profile** (a wrong database, host, port, user or password):
140... re-run the same `add-sql-server` command under the same `-s` name with every
141... field, the corrected one included, plus `--replace` and `--json`. That updates
142... the profile in place, so the project's `source_connection` still names it. Do
143... not remove and re-add it. Without `--replace` the CLI refuses the name with
144... `CNX0002` and keeps the old profile. Never pipe `add-sql-server` through `tail`
145... or `head`. Read its JSON: unless it says `"success":true`, the correction was
146... not saved, so surface the error instead of re-testing.
147... 
148... Do not use `docker exec`, `sqlcmd -P`, `echo`, or `printf` with a password to
149... diagnose this connection. Use `scai connection test` through `configure` below.
150... When the user already supplied a database, do not enumerate databases first.
151... 
152... ### Step 4: Save and Test Source Connection
153... 
154... When Step 1b already followed the SPCS Windows authentication reference, that file already called `configure`. Use its result for the checkpoint below. Do not call `configure` again on this visit.
155... 
156... Otherwise call the `configure` tool with `source_connection` set to `<SOURCE_CONNECTION_NAME>`. The MCP server runs `scai connection test` internally and only persists the connection if the test passes.
157... 
158... - **On success:** the response includes `connection_test: ok`.
159... - **On failure:** the tool returns an error containing the scai message. Surface it to the user, help them fix the issue, then re-run `configure(source_connection=<SOURCE_CONNECTION_NAME>)`. See `./references/REFERENCE.md` for troubleshooting.
160... - **SPCS Windows authentication, and this machine cannot sign in:** apply **When the local test cannot pass** in [`../../data-infrastructure/references/sqlserver-spcs-windows-auth.md`](../../data-infrastructure/references/sqlserver-spcs-windows-auth.md). When they choose "only the SPCS worker", the profile stays saved and this checkpoint does not require `connection_test: ok`.
161... - **`OpenSSL library could not be loaded` on macOS** (ODBC Driver 17 or 18): follow "macOS: the ODBC driver can't load OpenSSL" in `./references/REFERENCE.md`: check where Homebrew's `openssl` alias points, lead with the tested no-`sudo` `DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH` step, label the alias repoint "likely, unverified", and never offer links into `/usr/local/lib`; then re-test. Do not upgrade `msodbcsql18`. Switching to Direct does not avoid it: `--direct` reads the source with the same mssql-python driver as the worker, and a working `query_source` (.NET SqlClient) proves nothing about that driver.
162... - **`Cannot open database "<name>" requested by the login`** (SQL Server 4060, even when it ends "Login failed for user"): the sign-in was accepted; that database is missing or the login isn't mapped to it. Say exactly that. Do not ask for the password again, do not re-run `configure`, and do not create probe profiles on other databases. Follow "Cannot open database (4060)" in `./references/REFERENCE.md`: ask via `ask_user_question` *"May I list the databases `<USERNAME>` can open on this server?"* (**List them** / **I'll type the name**); on yes, run its one read-only `scai query ... --database master`, show the list and ask which to use, even when only one is listed. **Wait for the user's response — do not proceed until they choose.** Never change a connection's database without the user's confirmation: everything extracted without `-d` comes from that database. Then correct the profile with `--replace --json` and re-run `configure` once.
163... 
164... ## CHECKPOINT
165... 
166... Confirm with user:
167... - [ ] `configure` returned `connection_test: ok`, or the SPCS Windows path left the profile saved because this machine cannot sign in
168... - [ ] Connection appears in `scai connection list -l sqlserver --json`
169... - [ ] SPCS Windows path: `credentialsMaskedJson` includes `kerberos_principal`
170... - [ ] Source connection saved to session config when the test passed
171... 
172... ## On Completion
173... 
174... After the CHECKPOINT passes with `connection_test: ok`, tell the user:
175... > **Connection configured** — Successfully connected to SQL Server using connection `<connection_name>`.
176... 
177... When the SPCS Windows path saved the profile and this machine could not sign in, tell the user:
178... > **Connection profile saved** — `<connection_name>` is ready for the Snowpark Container Services worker. This machine is not the session source until a sign-in from here succeeds.
179... 
180... Then return to the calling skill.
181... 
182... ## Security Rules
183... 
184... - **NEVER** log or display passwords in plain text
185... - **NEVER** include passwords in command-line arguments that might be logged
186... - **NEVER** repeat a user-supplied password in a Bash tool call, including
187...   `--password`, `sqlcmd -P`, `docker exec`, `echo`, or `printf`
188... - **NEVER** write the password characters in an assistant message. Saying you
189...   will not inline it is still a repeat when the value appears. Say "the supplied
190...   password"
191... - In CI, reference an existing secret environment variable by name; never
192...   interpolate its value into agent-authored command text
193... - Use interactive mode or credential managers to avoid password exposure
194... 
195... ## Quick Reference
196... 
197... | Action | Command |
198... |--------|---------|
199... | Add connection (interactive) | `scai connection add-sql-server` |
200... | Add connection (inline, SQL auth) | `scai connection add-sql-server -s NAME --auth standard --server-url HOST --database DB --user USER` |
201... | Add connection (Windows auth) | `scai connection add-sql-server -s NAME --auth windows --server-url HOST --database DB` |
202... | Correct a saved connection | the same `add-sql-server` command with every field, plus `--replace --json` |
203... | Test connection | `configure(source_connection=NAME)` (runs the test internally) |
204... | List databases the login can open (after asking) | `scai query -s NAME --database master -q "SELECT name FROM sys.databases WHERE database_id > 4 AND HAS_DBACCESS(name) = 1 ORDER BY name" --json` |
205... | Set default | `scai connection set-default -l sqlserver -s NAME` |
206...
